hld:leaderboard.prompt: A sorted set of 10M players takes about 1 GB in Redis, so roughly 100 B per member. A new title expects 50M players on a single all-time board. About how much memory does that one board need?
options: About 500 MB
About 5 GB
About 50 GB
About 1 GB
hld:leaderboard.explanation: 1 GB / 10M is about 100 B per member (member string, score, skip-list and hash-table overhead). 50M x 100 B = 5 GB. 50 GB would assume 1 KB per member, ten times the measured cost.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: The score service applies 5,000 ZINCRBY calls per second around the clock. Roughly how many sorted-set updates does Redis absorb per day?
options: About 43 million
About 4.3 billion
About 430 million
About 4.3 million
hld:leaderboard.explanation: 5,000/s x 86,400 s/day = 432,000,000, about 430 million updates per day. 43 million would be the result of using 8,640 seconds per day, a factor-of-ten slip.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: A player has 300 friends and wants a friends-only leaderboard. Scores already live in one global sorted set. Which approach is the most practical?
options: Keep a separate sorted set of friends for every player and ZINCRBY into each friend's set on every score change
Read the 300 friends' scores from the global set in one ZMSCORE call and sort those 300 values in the service
Page through the whole global set with ZREVRANGE and keep only the entries that belong to friends
Run SELECT ... ORDER BY score over the scores DB filtered by the friend list on every page view
hld:leaderboard.explanation: With a bounded friend list, a single ZMSCORE (Redis 6.2+) or pipelined ZSCOREs returns 300 scores, and sorting 300 numbers is trivial. Per-player friend boards multiply every score write by the friend count, a fan-out cost that grows with the social graph.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: Why can Redis answer ZREVRANK in O(log N) for a sorted set of 10M members instead of counting members one by one?
options: Skip-list links store spans (nodes skipped), and the rank is summed while descending
Each update rewrites a precomputed rank stored in a hash next to every member of the set
The sorted set is kept as a binary heap, and a member's array index is its current rank
Redis caches the last ZREVRANK result per member and invalidates those entries on writes
hld:leaderboard.explanation: Redis skip-list links carry spans, so walking from the head to a node accumulates its rank in O(log N). A precomputed rank per member would need O(N) rewrites whenever a score near the top changes, which is the cost the span trick avoids.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: Points never exceed 1,000,000 and a season lasts under 10^7 seconds. On each update you recompute a composite score and write it with ZADD. Which encoding makes ZREVRANGE rank equal points by who reached them first, while staying exact in a double?
options: points x 10^7 + secondsSinceSeasonStart
points + secondsSinceSeasonStart / 10^7
points x 10^7 + (10^7 - 1 - secondsSinceSeasonStart)
Keep points as the score and prefix the member name with an ISO timestamp
hld:leaderboard.explanation: Subtracting the time from a constant makes an earlier time give a larger composite, so it ranks higher in descending order; the maximum 10^13 is below 2^53, so the double is exact. Adding the raw time does the opposite: the later player wins the tie. A timestamp member prefix also puts later players first, because ZREVRANGE orders equal scores by reverse lexicographic member.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: Prizes go to the weekly top 100 at Sunday 23:59:59. Game servers can deliver score events up to 30 seconds late. How should the winners be decided?
options: Read ZREVRANGE 0 99 at exactly 23:59:59 and award whatever the live sorted set shows then
Wait one hour after the cutoff, then award from the live sorted set as it stands at that moment
Snapshot the live board every minute and award from whichever snapshot shows the most players
Count only events timed before the cutoff, wait a grace window, then rank from durable history
hld:leaderboard.explanation: Prize boards need event-time semantics: late but valid events must count and post-cutoff events must not. Reading the live set at the cutoff drops events still in flight, and reading it an hour later includes scores earned after the deadline.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: A game server times out on POST /v1/scores {playerId, delta: 25} and retries, but the first request had actually succeeded. What happens, and what is the best fix?
options: Nothing changes, because ZINCRBY is idempotent for the same member and the same increment value
The second call fails, because Redis rejects two increments to one member within a second
The player gains 50 points; the fix is a longer client timeout so that retries never happen
The player gains 50; send a unique eventId and apply ZINCRBY only if that id is new, atomically
hld:leaderboard.explanation: ZINCRBY is not idempotent, so a retried delta double-counts. Deduplicating by event id (for example SET NX on the id plus ZINCRBY in one Lua script or MULTI) gives an exactly-once effect. A longer timeout makes retries rarer but cannot eliminate them.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: A board shows each player's best single-match score, not a running total. Which Redis command records a new match result correctly?
options: ZINCRBY board score player
ZADD board NX score player
ZADD board GT score player
ZADD board XX score player
hld:leaderboard.explanation: ZADD with GT (Redis 6.2+) only updates an existing member when the new score is greater and still adds new members, which is exactly 'keep the best'. NX never updates existing members, so a player's first score would stick forever; ZINCRBY sums scores.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: A 100M-player board is sharded by score range: shard 1 holds the highest scores, shard 2 the next band, and so on. How do you compute a player's exact global rank?
options: Sum ZCARD of all higher-band shards, then add the player's ZREVRANK in its own shard
Call ZREVRANK for the player on every shard and add the per-shard results together
Use ZREVRANK in the player's own shard only, since the score bands never overlap
Scan the top shard with ZREVRANGE, then each next shard, until the player is found
hld:leaderboard.explanation: Everyone in a higher band outranks the player, so the count of those shards (ZCARD, O(1) each) plus the in-shard rank gives the exact rank. The player exists in only one shard, so ZREVRANK elsewhere returns nil, and the in-shard rank alone ignores everyone above.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: The game now keeps daily, weekly, monthly and per-region boards, and Redis memory is growing fast. Which measures reduce memory without breaking current boards? Select all that apply.
options: Set an expiry on finished seasonal boards and keep their final standings as a snapshot in the database
Trim boards where only the top matters with ZREMRANGEBYRANK so they keep, say, the top 10,000
Store each board in a different Redis logical database number
Serve rarely viewed historical boards from database snapshots instead of live sorted sets
hld:leaderboard.explanation: Expiring finished boards, trimming top-only boards and serving cold history from the DB all cut resident memory. Logical database numbers are just namespaces in the same process and save nothing.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: Select all statements that are correct about Redis sorted set operations used by the leaderboard API.
options: ZREVRANGE board 0 99 WITHSCORES costs about O(log N + 100)
ZINCRBY on a member that does not exist creates it with the increment as its score
ZREVRANK of a member that is not in the set returns nil
ZCARD is O(N) because Redis counts the members on every call
hld:leaderboard.explanation: Range reads cost O(log N + M), ZINCRBY creates missing members starting from 0, and ZREVRANK returns nil for absent members. ZCARD is O(1) because the sorted set stores its length.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: Each player has a home region, and the product shows both a global and a per-region top 100. Select all sound design choices.
options: Apply ZINCRBY to both the global and the region sorted set in one pipeline or MULTI per score event
Keep a separate sorted set per region so regional ranks are direct ZREVRANK calls
When a player changes region, ZREM them from the old regional set and ZADD them to the new one with their current score
Build each region's top 100 by paging the global set and filtering until 100 players of that region appear
hld:leaderboard.explanation: Writing both sets per event keeps them consistent, per-region sets make regional ranks O(log N), and a region move needs an explicit remove and add. Filtering the global set can scan millions of entries for a small region before finding 100 players.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: Redis sorted set scores are IEEE 754 doubles, so integer scores larger than 2^53 can lose precision and tie or reorder unexpectedly.
options: True
False
hld:leaderboard.explanation: True. A double has a 53-bit significand, so integers beyond 2^53 cannot all be represented exactly. Composite scores (points plus a time component) must stay below that bound.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: Redis Top-K (RedisBloom) can return the exact global rank of any player, so it can replace the sorted set for 'your rank is 1,204'.
options: True
False
hld:leaderboard.explanation: False. Top-K is a probabilistic structure that tracks approximate heavy hitters in fixed memory. It answers 'who is roughly in the top K', not the exact rank of an arbitrary player.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: At peak 5M users are online, and each has a loc:{userId} entry of about 100 B in the Redis location cache. Roughly how much memory does the cache need, before replication?
options: About 50 MB
About 500 MB
About 5 GB
About 50 GB
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: 5M x 100 B = 500,000,000 B, about 500 MB, which fits in RAM on a small Redis cluster. 5 GB would assume 1 KB per entry, ten times the stated size.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Each WebSocket gateway can hold 50,000 idle sockets, and you want gateways at no more than 60% of that at the 2M-connection peak. About how many gateways do you need?
options: About 40
About 25
About 100
About 67
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: Usable capacity per gateway is 50,000 x 0.6 = 30,000, so 2,000,000 / 30,000 is about 67 gateways. 40 is the count at 100% utilisation, which leaves no room for a node failure or a reconnect surge.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Of 1M online users, 600k are stationary. Moving users send a location every 30 s and stationary users switch to every 120 s. About how many location updates per second remain, versus 33k with a fixed 30 s interval?
options: About 18k/s
About 25k/s
About 8k/s
About 30k/s
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: 400,000 / 30 is about 13.3k/s and 600,000 / 120 = 5k/s, so the total is about 18.3k/s, roughly 45% less than 33k/s, and fan-out shrinks by the same factor. 25k/s would come from cutting stationary users only to 60 s.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Why does the receiving gateway, not the publisher, check whether a friend's new location is within the radius?
options: Each subscriber has its own position and radius, so each receiver checks the one published point
Redis pub/sub can filter delivered messages by geographic distance on the server side itself
The publisher's location may be forged, so only the receiving side can trust the coordinates
Haversine is too expensive to run on the location service but is cheap on the gateways
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: The publisher does a single O(1) publish without knowing where each friend is; every receiving gateway compares the point with its own subscriber's last location and radius. Redis pub/sub has no content or geo filtering, it delivers every message to every subscriber.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: A celebrity user has 5,000 friends, many online at once. What is the best way to keep the system healthy?
options: Raise the location interval for every user to 5 minutes so total fan-out drops across the board
Move this user's updates to a dedicated Kafka topic with 5,000 partitions, one per friend
Disable heartbeats for this user's connections so the gateways spend less work on them
Share live location with a capped set of friends (say 500) and serve the rest on demand
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: The cost is subscriptions on connect and deliveries per publish, both proportional to online friends. Capping the shared set bounds that cost while on-demand lookups keep the feature usable. Slowing everyone down punishes millions of normal users for one outlier.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: One Redis pub/sub node in the cluster dies. What do users see, and how does the system recover?
options: All missed messages are replayed from the node's backlog once a replica has been promoted
Every user is disconnected and must log in again, because the channel state has been lost
Nothing is visible, since pub/sub messages are synchronously replicated to all nodes first
Friends on that node freeze briefly; gateways resubscribe and the next ping refreshes them
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: Pub/sub keeps no history, so updates on the dead node are simply lost; gateways detect the broken connection, look up the new owner and resubscribe, and the next periodic update repaints the friend. There is no backlog to replay.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Product wants to add 'people nearby who are not friends', for users who explicitly opt in. Which design fits?
options: Per-cell channels on a geohash-style grid; subscribe to your cell and its neighbours
Subscribe every opted-in user to the channels of all other users in the same country
Run a SQL distance query over every user's latest location row on each incoming ping
Reuse the friend channels and add nearby strangers to the friend list as temporary friends
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: Without a friend list to bound the candidates, you need a spatial index: per-cell channels plus the 8 neighbours cover the radius, and coarse locations limit privacy risk. Country-wide subscriptions would deliver millions of irrelevant messages per user.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Why does the friends feature not need a geohash or quadtree index at all?
options: Redis already stores every coordinate as a geohash internally, so the index exists for free
Friends almost always live in the same city, so a distance calculation is rarely needed
The friend list bounds candidates to about 40 online friends, so per-friend distance is cheap
Quadtrees cannot handle moving points, and geohashes are too coarse for a 5-mile radius
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: A spatial index exists to avoid checking every point; here the candidates are only a user's online friends, so a haversine per delivery is cheap. Quadtrees can track moving points but would add a rebuild cost for no gain.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Which change most reduces the risk that a friend pinpoints where a user lives by watching distance updates over time?
options: Serve the WebSocket only over TLS so that nobody on the network path can read positions
Lower the loc:{userId} cache TTL from 90 s to 60 s so that stale positions vanish sooner
Show distance in coarse buckets from a grid-snapped location, and limit how often it changes
Hash user ids in the pub/sub channel names so a friend cannot tell whose channel is whose
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: A malicious friend is an authorised recipient, so transport encryption or opaque ids do not help; reducing precision (grid snapping, distance buckets) and how often values update removes the signal needed to triangulate.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: A client connects and sends {type:'init'}. Select all statements that correctly describe the init flow.
options: The server loads the user's friend list from the friendship store or its cache
Friend locations are read from loc:{friendId} keys in one pipelined batch
The server queries location_history in Cassandra for every friend's last position
Friends whose loc key has expired are left out, since they are treated as offline
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: Init reads the friend list, then pipelines the cache reads; expired keys mean the friend is inactive and is omitted. History is optional, kept only for trails or analytics, and is not on the init path.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: The team proposes shortening the location interval from 30 s to 10 s. Select all consequences.
options: Pub/sub deliveries per second roughly triple
Phone battery and radio usage go up
The location cache size in memory stays about the same
The number of pub/sub subscriptions per connection triples
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: Three times as many pings means three times the fan-out and more battery drain, but the cache holds one overwritten entry per user and subscriptions depend on the online friend count, not on the ping rate.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Pub/sub channels are spread over a cluster of Redis nodes. Select all statements that are correct.
options: With consistent hashing, adding a node moves only a fraction of the channels
A single gateway typically holds connections to many pub/sub nodes, since its users' friends' channels are spread across them
Classic PUBLISH in Redis Cluster is broadcast to every node, which is why Redis 7 added sharded pub/sub (SPUBLISH)
Channels keep their recent messages through a node restart, so subscribers can catch up
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: Consistent hashing limits remapping, and gateways need connections to whichever nodes own their subscribed channels. Classic cluster pub/sub propagates every message cluster-wide, so Redis 7 sharded pub/sub keeps a channel on its slot's shard. Pub/sub stores nothing, so a restart loses messages.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Because location data is ephemeral, the location cache can run without persistence, accepting that a Redis restart briefly empties nearby lists until the next pings arrive.
options: True
False
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: True. Every online client rewrites its key within about 30 s, so the cache refills itself; the requirements favour availability over durability for live location.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Two points whose geohashes share a long prefix are close together, and conversely two points that are close together always share a long geohash prefix.
options: True
False
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: False. A shared prefix implies proximity, but the converse fails at cell boundaries: two points a metre apart on either side of a major boundary can share almost no prefix. That is why radius queries also scan the 8 neighbouring cells.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: A viewport needs 16 tiles. Raster tiles average about 100 KB and vector tiles about 30 KB. Roughly how much data does one full viewport load save by using vector tiles?
options: About 70 KB
About 1.1 MB
About 0.5 MB
About 11 MB
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Raster: 16 x 100 KB = 1.6 MB; vector: 16 x 30 KB = 480 KB; the saving is about 1.1 MB per viewport. 70 KB is the saving for a single tile, not the whole viewport.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: The pyramid has 4^z tiles at zoom level z. About how many tiles exist at zoom level 15 alone?
options: About 32 thousand
About 32 million
About 1 trillion
About 1 billion
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: 4^15 = 2^30, which is about 1.07 billion tiles. 32 thousand is 2^15, the number of tiles along one axis at that zoom, not the total.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: At peak there are 50,000 route requests per second, and a contraction-hierarchy query takes about 2 ms of CPU on one core. What is the minimum number of cores needed, before headroom?
options: About 25
About 1,000
About 100
About 400
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: 50,000 queries/s x 0.002 s = 100 core-seconds per second, so at least 100 busy cores, and in practice about double that for headroom and replicas per region. 25 would assume 0.5 ms per query.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: GPS points from a phone are noisy, and a highway runs right above a parallel service road. How should pings be matched to road edges?
options: Snap each point independently to the nearest road segment, since that is cheap and local
Discard every point that lies more than 5 m from a road, and snap the rest to the nearest one
Average all points of the trip into one location, then match that point to the nearest road
Score candidate segment sequences by GPS distance and route plausibility (HMM with Viterbi)
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Map matching scores whole sequences: a path that jumps between the highway and the service road every second is implausible, so the HMM picks a consistent route. Independent nearest-road snapping flips between parallel roads whenever noise moves a point.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: A bridge closes suddenly. How should routing reflect it within a minute or two?
options: Mark the edge closed in a live weight overlay, re-customise shortcuts, reroute affected sessions
Wait for the next map data release, then rebuild the regional graph and its shortcuts offline
Purge all CDN tiles in the region so that every client reloads the map and sees the closure
Lower the bridge's speed limit in the static graph file, then restart all the routing nodes
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Closures are a weight change, not a topology rebuild: a live overlay plus fast re-customisation (customisable contraction hierarchies) applies it quickly, and sessions indexed on that edge get rerouted. A full rebuild or map release takes hours or days.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: A user asks for the ETA of a trip that departs in one hour. Which computation fits best?
options: Use current live speeds on every edge of the route, since they are the freshest data available
Use historical speeds for that weekday and time, evaluated when the car reaches each edge
Use posted speed limits only, because traffic one hour from now cannot be known in advance
Reuse the ETA computed yesterday for an identical trip, since daily patterns repeat closely
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Live traffic says little about conditions an hour from now, so time-dependent historical profiles evaluated along the predicted trajectory are the best estimate. Speed limits ignore well-known daily congestion patterns.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: A user types '1600 Amphitheatre Pkwy'. Which index answers this geocoding request?
options: A B-tree index on (lat, lng) in the routing database, searched around the user's position
A geohash prefix scan that uses the typed address text as the prefix to look up
The road graph adjacency lists, searched outward from the user's current position
An inverted index over normalised address tokens, ranked by match and proximity
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Geocoding is text search: tokenised, normalised addresses in an inverted index, with geo filtering or boosting. A lat/lng B-tree or geohash only works once you already know the coordinates.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: Why does the client batch location pings to POST /v1/location-batch, and why does the server answer 202?
options: Batching is required by HTTP/2, and 202 means the batch was rejected
Batching lets the server route without a WebSocket, and 202 confirms the ETA was updated
Batching cuts radio wake-ups and request overhead, and 202 means accepted for asynchronous processing
Batching guarantees ordering, and 202 means each ping was matched to a road
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Fewer, larger uploads save battery and bandwidth on mobile, and the pings go into Kafka for later map matching, so the server acknowledges acceptance (202) rather than completed processing.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: Map matching needs the consecutive points of one trip, while speed aggregation needs all observations of one road edge. How should the pipeline key its data?
options: Key raw pings by session for matching, then re-key matched records by edge_id to aggregate
Key everything by edge_id from the start, so both stages read the same single topic
Use round-robin partitioning, since both stages can query a database for missing context
Key everything by user id, and have the aggregator scan all partitions in every window
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Each stage needs its own locality: per-trip order for map matching, per-edge grouping for aggregation, so you re-partition between them. Raw pings cannot be keyed by edge_id because the edge is only known after map matching.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: Select all correct statements about contraction hierarchies (CH) and live traffic.
options: Shortcut costs are computed from edge weights at preprocessing time, so changed weights can make them stale
Customisable variants split slow, metric-independent preprocessing from a fast step that re-applies new weights
A CH query returns an approximate route that can be noticeably longer than the true shortest path
Bidirectional search, which CH queries use, reduces explored nodes compared with a one-directional search
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: CH queries are exact for the weights used in preprocessing; the issue is that live traffic changes those weights, which customisable CH addresses with a fast re-weighting step. The upward and downward bidirectional search keeps queries tiny.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: Select all sound choices for tile generation and caching.
options: Versioned, immutable tile URLs so CDN caches can use very long max-age
Pre-generate low zooms and render high zooms on first request, then cache them
Pre-render all 21 zoom levels for the whole planet before launch
Use vector tiles so a theme change is restyled on the client without new tiles
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Versioned URLs, lazy high zooms and client-side styling keep storage and bandwidth low. Zoom 21 alone is about 4.4 trillion tiles, mostly ocean and empty land, so pre-rendering everything wastes enormous storage.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: There are 5M active navigation sessions, and traffic updates arrive every minute. Select all practices that keep rerouting affordable.
options: Index active sessions by the edges remaining on their route
Recompute only sessions whose upcoming edges have slowed significantly
Recompute a fresh route for all 5M sessions on every traffic update
Push a new route only when it saves more than a set threshold
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: An edge-to-session index turns a traffic change into a targeted set of recomputations, and a savings threshold avoids churn. Recomputing all 5M every minute would demand about 83k route queries per second just for refreshes, nearly all of them returning the same route.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm requires non-negative edge weights, which travel times on road segments satisfy.
options: True
False
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: True. Dijkstra's greedy settling of nodes is correct only with non-negative weights, and travel time on a road can never be negative.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: Because ETAs use live traffic, the base map tiles must be re-rendered every minute so that roads show their current congestion colour.
options: True
False
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: False. Traffic is a separate, small overlay layer refreshed independently; base tiles stay immutable per map version and keep their long CDN cache lifetimes.

hld:message-queue.prompt: A cluster ingests 1M messages/s of about 1 KB each, keeps 3 days of retention and uses replication factor 3. Roughly how much disk does it need?
options: About 260 TB
About 780 TB
About 1.8 PB
About 78 TB
hld:message-queue.explanation: 1 GB/s x 259,200 s (3 days) is about 259 TB raw; x3 replicas is about 780 TB. 260 TB forgets replication, and 1.8 PB is the 7-day figure.

hld:message-queue.prompt: The cluster must store 1.8 PB including replicas. Each broker has 20 TB of disk, and you keep disks at most 70% full. About how many brokers are needed?
options: About 130
About 90
About 180
About 65
hld:message-queue.explanation: Usable per broker = 20 TB x 0.7 = 14 TB; 1,800 TB / 14 TB is about 129 brokers. 90 assumes 100% fill, leaving no room for growth, rebalancing or a failed broker's data.

hld:message-queue.prompt: A new consumer starts replaying data from two days ago, and producer and tail-consumer latency spike for everyone on those brokers. What is the most likely cause?
options: The replaying consumer holds a read lock on the partition that blocks producers from appending
Reading old offsets triggers log compaction on those segments, which pauses incoming writes
Cold reads miss the page cache, hit disk and evict hot tail pages, so everyone competes for IO
Zero-copy transfer is disabled automatically for offsets older than a day, slowing the broker
hld:message-queue.explanation: Brokers rely on the OS page cache for recent data. A large historical scan pulls cold segments from disk and pushes hot pages out, so tail reads and writes start hitting disk too. Partitions have no reader locks; readers never block producers.

hld:message-queue.prompt: With acks=1, a partition leader acknowledges a message and then crashes before any follower fetched it. A follower becomes leader. What happens to that message?
options: It is safe, because acks=1 waits until at least one follower has also stored the message
It is delivered twice to consumers, once from the old leader and once from the new leader
The producer is notified of the loss by the controller and resends the message automatically
It is lost: the new leader never had it, and the old leader truncates its log on rejoining
hld:message-queue.explanation: acks=1 waits for the leader only, so an acknowledged but unreplicated message vanishes on failover; the producer has no reason to resend. acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 closes that window.

hld:message-queue.prompt: A producer has retries enabled, allows 5 in-flight requests per connection, and has idempotence disabled. Batch 1 fails transiently, batch 2 succeeds, then the retry of batch 1 succeeds. What is the result?
options: The broker holds batch 2 back until batch 1 arrives, so the original order is always kept
Batch 1's retry is dropped by the broker as a duplicate, so its records are lost entirely
Both batches are written in their original order, because the producer assigns the offsets
Batch 2 lands before batch 1; idempotent-producer sequence numbers would prevent that
hld:message-queue.explanation: Without idempotence the broker appends batches as they arrive, so a retry can land after a later batch. With idempotence, per-partition sequence numbers let the broker reject out-of-order batches, keeping order with up to 5 in-flight requests.

hld:message-queue.prompt: Every in-sync replica of a partition is down, and only an out-of-sync follower is alive. unclean.leader.election.enable is false. What happens?
options: The out-of-sync follower becomes leader and fetches the missing messages from producers later
It stays unavailable until an ISR replica returns; unclean election would trade loss for uptime
The controller merges the logs of all replicas, including offline ones, into a new leader
Producers keep writing to a temporary partition that the controller creates automatically
hld:message-queue.explanation: With unclean election disabled, Kafka-style systems prefer consistency: no leader from outside the ISR, so no lost acknowledged data, at the price of availability. Enabling it promotes a stale replica and truncates the messages it missed.

hld:message-queue.prompt: A compacted topic holds the latest profile per user id. How do you delete user 42's profile from it?
options: Produce key 42 with a null value (a tombstone), which compaction honours
Call the admin API to remove the record stored at user 42's latest offset
Stop producing for key 42 and wait for time-based retention to drop it
Produce key 42 with an empty JSON object as the value to clear the profile
hld:message-queue.explanation: Compaction keeps the latest value per key, so a null-value tombstone is the latest value and marks the key deleted. An empty object is still a real value, and the key would keep existing forever.

hld:message-queue.prompt: Consumer lag grows steadily on partition 7 while the other 31 partitions of the topic stay near zero. What is the most likely cause?
options: A hot key skews traffic onto partition 7, or its single consumer is slow
The topic has too many partitions overall, so the group spreads too thin
The producer uses acks=all, which slows writes to the partition leaders
Log compaction is enabled on the topic and is rewriting older segments
hld:message-queue.explanation: Lag on one partition only points at skew, either in data (a hot key hashing there) or in its one assigned consumer. A cluster-wide setting such as acks or partition count would affect every partition, not just one.

hld:message-queue.prompt: Why do Kafka-style brokers let consumers pull data rather than pushing it to them?
options: Pull always gives lower end-to-end latency than push, whatever the load or batch size
Pull removes the need for consumers or brokers to store committed offsets at all
Pull guarantees exactly-once delivery, because each record is fetched only once
Consumers set their own pace and batch size, giving backpressure and easy replay
hld:message-queue.explanation: With pull, a slow consumer just falls behind instead of being overwhelmed, it can fetch large batches, and it can rewind. Push can have lower latency, which is why the trade-off exists, so 'lower latency in every case' is wrong.

hld:message-queue.prompt: A consumer reads orders and writes rows to PostgreSQL. Which approaches give an effectively-once effect on the database? Select all that apply.
options: Store the processed partition offset in the same database transaction as the rows, and resume from it on restart
Make the write an idempotent upsert keyed by a unique message or business id
Use Kafka transactions, which make the PostgreSQL write atomic with the offset commit
Commit the offset before writing the rows
hld:message-queue.explanation: Atomically storing offsets with the side effect, or making the side effect idempotent, both make redelivery harmless. Kafka transactions only cover writes inside Kafka, not an external database, and committing first gives at-most-once.

hld:message-queue.prompt: A team wants to raise a topic from 50 to 5,000 partitions 'just in case'. Select all real costs.
options: More segment and index files open on brokers
Longer leader elections and recovery when a broker fails, since more partitions need new leaders
More producer memory for per-partition batch buffers, and smaller batches per partition
Messages within one partition lose their ordering guarantee
hld:message-queue.explanation: Each partition adds files, metadata, failover work and producer batches, so oversizing costs throughput and recovery time. Ordering within a partition is unchanged by partition count; only the key-to-partition mapping changes.

hld:message-queue.prompt: Select all correct statements about how a partition is stored on disk.
options: Only the newest (active) segment is appended to; older segments are immutable
A sparse offset index lets the broker binary-search to a nearby position and scan forward to the requested offset
Time-based retention deletes whole closed segments rather than individual records
A single message in the middle of a segment of a non-compacted topic can be deleted in place through the produce API
hld:message-queue.explanation: Segments are append-only, indexed sparsely, and retired whole, which keeps IO sequential and deletion cheap. There is no in-place deletion of a single record in a delete-policy topic.

hld:message-queue.prompt: Raising the producer's linger.ms usually increases throughput but adds per-message latency, because records wait longer to fill larger batches.
options: True
False
hld:message-queue.explanation: True. Larger batches amortise per-request overhead and compress better, at the cost of records waiting up to linger.ms before being sent.

hld:message-queue.prompt: Setting acks=0 still gives at-least-once delivery, because the broker retries any write that failed on its side.
options: True
False
hld:message-queue.explanation: False. With acks=0 the producer does not wait for any response, so it cannot know a write failed and never retries it; this is at-most-once.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: You keep one year of 5-minute rollups for 100M series, storing 4 aggregates (min, max, sum, count) per point at about 2 B each after compression. Roughly how much storage is that?
options: About 8.4 TB
About 84 TB
About 840 TB
About 2.5 TB
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: One year has 365 x 288 = 105,120 five-minute points per series. 100M x 105,120 x 8 B is about 8.4 x 10^13 B, about 84 TB. 8.4 TB drops a factor of ten in the series count.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: The alert evaluator runs 120,000 rules, each every 30 seconds. About how many rule queries per second hit recent data?
options: About 400
About 2,000
About 4,000
About 3.6 million
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: 120,000 / 30 s = 4,000 queries per second. 2,000 would be the rate for a 60-second interval.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: A metric has labels service (50 values), endpoint (200), status (10) and instance (100). In the worst case, how many series can it create?
options: About 360
About 100,000
About 1 million
About 10 million
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Series count multiplies across labels: 50 x 200 x 10 x 100 = 10,000,000. Adding the counts (360) is the common mistake; every unique combination is its own series.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Why do services export a monotonically increasing request counter and compute rate() at query time, rather than exporting 'requests in the last interval' as a gauge?
options: Counters take less memory than gauges on the target, so exporting them is cheaper
A missed scrape loses nothing; the next increase covers the gap, and drops mean resets
Gauges cannot be stored with XOR compression, so they cost far more disk in the TSDB
rate() is defined only for counters that never reset, which makes the query simpler
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Cumulative counters are robust to lost or delayed samples: the delta between any two samples is still right, and rate() treats a decrease as a counter reset. A per-interval gauge silently loses the requests of any missed scrape.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: In pull mode, a target process crashes and emits nothing at all. How does the system notice?
options: The failed scrape records up = 0, and an alert fires on up == 0 for a 'for' duration
It cannot notice, because absent data looks the same as a healthy but idle service
The target pushes a final 'goodbye' metric to the collector as part of crashing
The TSDB deletes the target's series right away, and the deletion triggers an alert
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: One advantage of pull is that the collector knows what should exist (via service discovery), so a failed scrape is itself a signal recorded as up = 0. A crashed process cannot reliably send a goodbye.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: An alert on 'error rate > 5%' with for: 0s pages on-call 30 times a night on 20-second spikes that are never actionable. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the threshold to 50% so that only very large incidents ever page anyone
Scrape the targets less often so short spikes are averaged away and less visible
Require the condition for several minutes, or better, alert on SLO burn rate
Route the alert to email instead of the pager so that it no longer wakes anyone
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: A 'for' window suppresses blips, and burn-rate alerts page on sustained user impact rather than noise. A 50% threshold would miss real incidents that hurt users at 10% errors.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: How does the TSDB find the series matching {service='api', status='500'} without scanning every series?
options: It range-scans all series names alphabetically and filters out non-matching ones
It intersects the postings lists (series ids) of each label pair in an inverted index
It hashes the whole label matcher to a single series id and looks that series up
It reads every block's chunks and filters the decoded samples by their labels
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: The inverted index maps each label=value pair to a sorted list of series ids, so a multi-label matcher is a fast intersection. Reading every chunk would be a full scan of the data.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Kubernetes pods are redeployed about 20 times a day, and every metric carries a pod label. Head-block memory and the index keep growing even though the live pod count is flat. What is happening, and what is the best remedy?
options: A memory leak in the TSDB process; schedule a restart every night to reclaim the memory
The scrape interval is too short; raise it to 60 s so fewer samples reach the head block
There are too many alert rules; delete unused ones so the evaluator holds less state
Series churn from new pod names; aggregate away the pod label for long-term data
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Every redeploy creates a new label value and so new series, while the old ones linger in the head block and index until they age out. Dropping or aggregating the churning label caps the series count; a nightly restart only hides the growth.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Samples arrive at timestamps 1000, 1010, 1020, 1030, 1041. Gorilla-style encoding stores the first timestamp and the first delta. Which delta-of-delta values are stored for the remaining three timestamps?
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Deltas are 10, 10, 10, 11, so the deltas of deltas for the third, fourth and fifth timestamps are 0, 0, 1. Zeros encode in a single bit, which is why regular scrapes compress so well. '10, 10, 11' are plain deltas, not deltas of deltas.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Rollups keep min, max, sum and count per 5-minute window. Select all statements that are correct.
options: The exact 1-hour average is sum of sums divided by sum of counts
The exact 1-hour maximum is the largest of the twelve 5-minute maxima
Keeping histogram bucket counters in the rollups allows approximate percentiles later
An exact p99 can be computed from the stored min, max and average
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Sum and count combine exactly into averages, and max of maxes is exact. Percentiles need distribution data such as histogram buckets; min, max and mean cannot reconstruct a p99.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Push ingestion is open to many teams. Select all protections against a misbehaving client flooding the pipeline.
options: Per-tenant rate limits on samples per second
Per-tenant active-series quotas
Reject over-limit requests with 429 so well-behaved clients back off and retry
Disable the write-ahead log during bursts to keep up
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Rate limits, series quotas and explicit 429 backpressure contain one bad client. Disabling the WAL protects nobody from the client and risks losing in-memory data on a crash.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Select all sound choices for making the TSDB horizontally scalable and multi-tenant.
options: Shard incoming series by a hash of tenant plus series labels across ingesters
Replicate each series to 2 or 3 ingesters so one failure loses no recent data
Have the query layer fan out to the relevant shards and merge the results
Shard by time only, so all current writes go to the node owning the current hour
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Hashing by series spreads write load, replication covers failures, and query fan-out merges results. Time-only sharding sends every current write to one hot node.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: The write-ahead log next to the in-memory head block lets the TSDB recover recent samples that had not yet been flushed into an immutable block when it crashed.
options: True
False
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: True. Samples are appended to the WAL before being acknowledged, so after a crash the head block is rebuilt by replaying it.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Total HTTP requests served should be exported as a gauge, because rate() only works on gauges.
options: True
False
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: False. Totals are counters, and rate() is designed for counters (it handles resets). Gauges are for values that go up and down, such as memory in use or queue depth.

hld:email-service.prompt: Assume 200M users each send 15 messages a day. Roughly what is the average outbound rate in messages per second?
options: About 3,500
About 35,000
About 350,000
About 12,000
hld:email-service.explanation: 200M x 15 = 3B messages/day; 3B / 86,400 s is about 34,700/s. 3,500 is off by a factor of ten.

hld:email-service.prompt: 2B messages arrive per day with about 1 KB of metadata each, kept for 5 years with replication factor 3. Roughly how much metadata storage is that?
options: About 3.7 PB
About 1.1 PB
About 11 PB
About 110 TB
hld:email-service.explanation: 2 TB/day x 365 x 5 is about 3,650 TB (3.65 PB); x3 replicas is about 11 PB. 3.7 PB forgets replication.

hld:email-service.prompt: A company newsletter with a 2 MB attachment is sent to 1M mailboxes on our service. Attachments are content-addressed by SHA-256. Roughly how much attachment storage does deduplication save?
options: About 2 TB
About 2 GB
About 200 GB
Nothing, since each mailbox needs its own copy
hld:email-service.explanation: Without dedup: 1M x 2 MB = 2 TB. With content addressing, one 2 MB blob plus 1M references is stored, saving about 2 TB. Mailboxes only need a pointer and a reference count, not a private copy.

hld:email-service.prompt: A simple forwarding service relays a message from bank.com to our users without modifying it. Which authentication result typically survives the forward?
options: SPF, because the forwarder copies the original sender's IP into the forwarded headers
Neither, because any forwarding hop always invalidates both SPF and DKIM checks
DKIM, because the signature over the unchanged headers and body still verifies
Both of them, as long as the forwarder delivers the message to us over TLS
hld:email-service.explanation: SPF checks the connecting IP, which is now the forwarder's and is not in bank.com's SPF record, so SPF fails. DKIM signs the content, so an unmodified message still verifies and DMARC can pass through DKIM alignment.

hld:email-service.prompt: Millions of IMAP clients keep IDLE connections open waiting for new mail. Which design scales?
options: Each IMAP server polls the metadata store for every connected user once per second
Clients drop IDLE and reconnect every 10 seconds to check for new messages instead
Event-driven servers subscribe to per-user change notifications and push on new mail
Each IMAP server keeps the full mailboxes of all its connected users in memory
hld:email-service.explanation: Idle connections are cheap on event-driven servers; the work should happen only when mail arrives, through a per-user notification channel. Polling every user every second would turn millions of idle clients into millions of reads per second.

hld:email-service.prompt: A newsletter goes to 5 million external subscribers. How should the pipeline treat it differently from a normal message?
options: Expand recipients into queued batches, rate-limited per domain, with VERP and List-Unsubscribe
Put all 5 million addresses into the RCPT TO list of a single SMTP transaction per domain
Send it from a fresh, unused IP so the main pool's sending reputation is not affected
Send it synchronously inside the API request so the sender gets one combined result
hld:email-service.explanation: Bulk mail must be spread over time and domains to avoid throttling, track bounces per recipient and give recipients an unsubscribe path, which protects reputation. A cold, unwarmed IP sending 5 million messages is quickly throttled or blocklisted.

hld:email-service.prompt: Bounce rates from one outbound IP suddenly spike, and replies cite a public blocklist. What is the right response?
options: Keep sending from the same IP so the receivers learn over time that it is legitimate
Shift traffic to other warmed IPs, suspend the abusive sender, then request delisting
Disable DKIM signing for mail from that IP until the listing expires on its own
Retry every rejected message immediately from the same IP until the receivers accept it
hld:email-service.explanation: The immediate fix is to stop using the blocked IP, the root cause is usually one abusive sender, and delisting comes after the cause is gone. Immediate retries from the same IP only deepen the reputation damage.

hld:email-service.prompt: Opening a message costs two hops (metadata row, then blob store), and p99 open latency suffers. Most messages are under 4 KB of text. What is the best change?
options: Move every body, including large attachments, into the metadata rows themselves
Inline bodies under a size threshold in the metadata row; keep pointers for the rest
Add a third cache tier in front of the blob store that holds every stored message
Drop the blob store and keep message bodies on the SMTP edge servers that received them
hld:email-service.explanation: Inlining small bodies removes a hop for the common case while large blobs stay out of the hot store. Inlining everything bloats the metadata partitions and the hot set, which hurts list queries.

hld:email-service.prompt: IMAP requires UIDs that strictly increase within a folder. Why does the design keep each folder's writes on a single partition owner?
options: So the owner can hand out the next UID from a local counter, with no coordination
Because wide-column stores cannot hold more than one folder per node at a time
So that each user's search index stays small enough to fit on a single node
Because SMTP requires exactly one server to be responsible for each recipient
hld:email-service.explanation: Monotonic UIDs need a single sequencer per folder; one owner makes allocation a cheap local increment. If several nodes wrote to a folder, they would need a distributed counter or locks on every delivery.

hld:email-service.prompt: A user's mailbox must move to a different shard without downtime. Select all steps of a sound migration.
options: Copy a snapshot of the mailbox to the new shard
Tail and apply changes made after the snapshot until the copy catches up
Briefly pause writes for that user, apply the final changes, then flip the routing entry to the new shard
Delete the source data before copying so the two cannot diverge
hld:email-service.explanation: Snapshot, catch up, then a short per-user cutover is the standard live migration. Deleting first risks losing the mailbox if the copy fails.

hld:email-service.prompt: Select all sound practices for spam filtering in the inbound pipeline.
options: Run cheap checks (rate limits, IP reputation, recipient exists) before expensive content scanning
Reject clear spam with a 5xx during the SMTP dialogue rather than bouncing it after acceptance
Send a bounce to the MAIL FROM address for every message found to be spam after acceptance
File likely spam into a Spam folder rather than deleting it, so false positives can be recovered
hld:email-service.explanation: Cheap checks first save compute, in-dialogue rejection avoids backscatter, and a Spam folder limits the cost of false positives. Bouncing accepted spam mails forged, innocent addresses.

hld:email-service.prompt: Select all correct statements about mailbox search in this design.
options: Each user's index lives on one shard, so a query touches a single shard
A single global index over all users makes per-user search cheaper than per-user shards
The indexer consumes delivery events, so search may lag delivery by a few seconds
A lost index shard can be rebuilt from the event log or the stored messages
hld:email-service.explanation: Per-user co-location avoids scatter-gather, asynchronous indexing means slight lag, and the index is derived data that can be rebuilt. A global index makes every user query filter a huge shared index.

hld:email-service.prompt: In SMTP, a 4xx reply tells the sending server to try again later, while a 5xx reply signals a permanent failure.
options: True
False
hld:email-service.explanation: True. 4xx codes (such as 451) are transient and trigger retries with backoff; 5xx codes (such as 550) are permanent and produce a bounce.

hld:email-service.prompt: For a message to pass DMARC, both SPF and DKIM must pass and both must align with the From domain.
options: True
False
hld:email-service.explanation: False. DMARC passes if either SPF or DKIM passes with alignment to the From domain. That is why DKIM alone can carry a forwarded message through DMARC.

hld:object-storage.prompt: A cluster stores 90 PB of usable data with a 6+3 erasure code on 20 TB drives kept at most 75% full. About how many drives are needed?
options: About 6,000
About 9,000
About 13,500
About 4,500
hld:object-storage.explanation: 6+3 stores 9/6 = 1.5x, so 135 PB raw. Each drive holds 20 TB x 0.75 = 15 TB usable; 135,000 TB / 15 TB = 9,000 drives. 6,000 forgets the parity overhead.

hld:object-storage.prompt: A cluster has 10,000 drives with an assumed 2% annual failure rate. Roughly how many drive failures should the repair system expect?
options: About 2 per year
About 20 per year
About 4 per week
About 2 per day
hld:object-storage.explanation: 10,000 x 0.02 = 200 failures a year, about 4 per week. At this scale repair is routine background work, not an exceptional event.

hld:object-storage.prompt: At peak there are 30,000 PUT/s of 4 MB objects, stored with an 8+4 erasure code. About how much data per second is written to data nodes, including parity?
options: About 120 GB/s
About 360 GB/s
About 60 GB/s
About 180 GB/s
hld:object-storage.explanation: Ingest is 30,000 x 4 MB = 120 GB/s. 8+4 writes 12/8 = 1.5x that, so about 180 GB/s reach the data nodes. 120 GB/s ignores the parity fragments.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Most objects in a bucket are 4 KB. Why is erasure coding each one separately with 8+4 a poor fit?
options: Erasure codes cannot mathematically encode objects that are smaller than 1 MB in size
Each becomes 12 fragments of about 512 B, so metadata and IOPS overhead dwarf the data
Small objects are almost always hot, and erasure-coded data cannot be cached at all
An 8+4 code stores four extra full copies of each small object instead of parity
hld:object-storage.explanation: Splitting a tiny object into 12 pieces multiplies index entries and disk operations for very little data. Packing small objects into large files before coding (or replicating them) keeps the overhead reasonable. The code itself works at any size; it is just inefficient.

hld:object-storage.prompt: One customer writes millions of keys under the single prefix logs/2024-06-01/, and the metadata range partition holding it is overloaded. What is the primary fix in the storage system?
options: Switch the whole metadata store from range partitioning to hash partitioning
Reject or heavily throttle further writes from that customer's account
Automatically split the hot key range into more partitions based on load
Put a CDN in front of the bucket so that the PUT requests are absorbed there
hld:object-storage.explanation: Range-partitioned stores split hot ranges dynamically, keeping ordered listing while spreading load. Hash partitioning would fix the hotspot but make every prefix listing a scatter-gather across all partitions.

hld:object-storage.prompt: A GET arrives for an 8+4 object while the node holding one of its data fragments is down. What happens?
options: The object is unavailable until the node holding that data fragment comes back
It reads any 8 of the 11 surviving fragments and decodes, at higher latency
It returns the 7 available data fragments to the client as a partial object
It sends all 11 surviving fragments to the client, which decodes them itself
hld:object-storage.explanation: Any 8 of 12 fragments reconstruct the object, so the read succeeds as a degraded read with extra decode work and IO. Decoding happens server-side; clients receive normal object bytes.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Why does each metadata shard replicate its writes through a consensus protocol such as Raft or Paxos?
options: So a LIST right after a PUT sees the new key, and acked writes survive a failure
To compress metadata rows by sharing common key prefixes across the replicas
To decide how object bytes are spread across the data nodes and racks
To let DELETE requests return immediately and be applied asynchronously later
hld:object-storage.explanation: Consensus gives each shard one linearisable order of writes, which delivers strong read-after-write for objects and listings and durability for acknowledged writes. Data placement is the data plane's job, separate from metadata replication.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Why does the garbage collector wait for a safety delay before deleting a blob that has no metadata row?
options: Disks need idle time between writes and deletes, so the GC spaces out its work
An in-flight PUT has written data but not yet metadata, so a quick delete could lose it
Customers are billed for a minimum storage period, so blobs are kept until it ends
Erasure coding requires every fragment to exist for a day before it can be removed
hld:object-storage.explanation: Data is written before the metadata commit, so 'no metadata row' can mean 'in flight', not 'orphan'. The delay also guards against GC bugs. Billing rules are a pricing policy and do not explain the delay.

hld:object-storage.prompt: A client starts many multipart uploads and never completes or aborts them. What happens to the uploaded parts?
options: They are deleted automatically as soon as the client's connection is closed
They become visible in listings as separate objects named after part numbers
They are merged into a partial object automatically after 24 hours of inactivity
They use storage until aborted, usually by a lifecycle rule for stale uploads
hld:object-storage.explanation: Parts are stored as real data objects tied to the upload, so they consume space until an abort, usually via a lifecycle rule. Parts are never visible as user objects before Complete.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Objects use 8+4 erasure coding with each stripe spread over 12 racks, and one whole rack goes down. Select all that hold.
options: Reads continue as degraded reads, since each stripe still has 11 fragments
Repair rebuilds the lost fragments onto other healthy racks, starting with stripes that have lost the most fragments
Repair traffic is throttled so it does not starve foreground requests
All writes must stop until the rack returns, since stripes need 12 racks
hld:object-storage.explanation: One lost fragment per stripe still leaves 3 more failures of tolerance; repair restores redundancy, prioritised and throttled. New writes can be placed on stripes across the remaining healthy failure domains, so there is no need to stop writes.

hld:object-storage.prompt: A client issues GET with Range: bytes=0-1048575 for a large object stored with a systematic 8+4 code, and all fragments are healthy. Select all statements that are true.
options: Only the data fragments covering that byte range need to be read
No decoding is needed, since data fragments contain the original bytes
The parity fragments must also be read and verified on every request
The response is 206 Partial Content
hld:object-storage.explanation: With a systematic code, data fragments hold the plain bytes, so a healthy range read touches only the relevant fragments and returns 206. Parity is used only when data fragments are missing or corrupt, and checksums cover integrity.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Select all statements that are correct about asynchronous cross-region replication.
options: It can be driven by a change stream of committed metadata writes
The destination region may lag, so its recovery point is not zero
It protects against a region-wide outage that in-region erasure coding cannot
It removes the need for erasure coding or replication within each region
hld:object-storage.explanation: Replaying committed changes to another region adds disaster protection with some lag. Each region still needs local redundancy for routine disk and rack failures; otherwise every drive failure would need a cross-region copy.

hld:object-storage.prompt: The 11 nines advertised for S3 Standard describe durability (the chance of losing an object), not availability (the chance of a request succeeding).
options: True
False
hld:object-storage.explanation: True. Durability of 99.999999999% is a data-loss design target; availability is a separate, much lower figure, because a temporarily unreachable object is not a lost one.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Storing each object as its own file on the data nodes scales well to billions of 1 KB objects, because modern filesystems have no practical inode or metadata limits.
options: True
False
hld:object-storage.explanation: False. Billions of tiny files strain inode tables and directory metadata and cause random IO; that is why data nodes pack many objects into large append-only files with their own index.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Assume 300M transfers a day, a peak of 6x the daily average, and about 1,500 transfers per second per shard. What is the minimum number of shards at peak?
options: About 4
About 21
About 14
About 140
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: 300M / 86,400 is about 3,470/s average; x6 is about 20,800/s at peak; / 1,500 per shard is about 13.9, so 14 shards at minimum. 21 would assume 1,000 per shard.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Transfers average about 12,000 per second, and balance reads run at about 8x writes. Roughly how many balance reads per second must be served?
options: About 1,500
About 96,000
About 960,000
About 20,000
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: 12,000 x 8 = 96,000 reads/s, served from the wallet row, replicas or caches for non-critical views, never by summing ledger history.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: The ledger grows by about 700 GB/day, and regulation requires keeping it for 7 years. Roughly how much ledger data is that before replication and indexes?
options: About 180 TB
About 5 PB
About 1.8 PB
About 250 TB
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: 700 GB x 365 is about 255 TB per year; x7 is about 1.8 PB. 250 TB is only one year of data.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Why are amounts stored as integer minor units (amount: 2500 for 25.00 USD) rather than floating-point numbers?
options: Integers take noticeably less disk space than floats in every major database
Binary floats cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift
JSON has no way to carry floating-point numbers between client and server
Relational databases cannot build indexes on floating-point columns at all
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Money needs exact arithmetic; integer cents (or a fixed decimal type) make sums and ledger checks exact. JSON does carry floats, which is exactly how precision bugs sneak in.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: In a TCC cross-shard transfer, Try placed a hold of 50 on the source wallet, then the destination wallet turns out to be closed. What should happen?
options: Cancel runs: the hold returns to the available balance and the transfer fails
Confirm runs anyway, and the money is parked in the closed destination wallet
The hold stays in place indefinitely until a support agent reviews it by hand
The source is debited in full and a refund is promised to the user by email
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: TCC's Cancel phase undoes the reservation idempotently, so no money moves and nothing is lost. Confirming into a closed wallet strands funds, and leaving holds wastes the user's available balance.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: The provider's daily settlement file is 1 cent higher than the ledger's total for top-ups. How should this be found and fixed?
options: Edit the most recent top-up ledger entry by 1 cent so the two totals match again
Ignore it, because a 1 cent difference is below any reasonable materiality level
Match settlement lines to entries by reference id, then post a compensating entry
Recompute every balance from scratch and overwrite the wallet table with the results
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Line-level matching finds the exact cause (a missing, duplicated or rounded item), and a compensating entry fixes it without rewriting history. Editing an existing entry breaks the immutable audit trail.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Wallets must move from 50 to 100 physical shards while transfers keep running. Which approach works best?
options: Change routing from hash mod 50 to hash mod 100 and restart every service at once
Use many logical partitions; move each by copy, catch-up and a brief write pause
Stop all transfers for a weekend, copy everything, then reopen on the new layout
Send new wallets to the new shards and leave all existing wallets where they are
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Logical partitions decouple keys from machines, so a move is a per-partition copy, catch-up and short cutover. Switching mod 50 to mod 100 remaps about half of all wallets at once, and in-flight transfers would hit the wrong shard.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Why does the wallet service write events to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the transfer, instead of publishing to Kafka directly after the commit?
options: Kafka cannot accept events directly from an application that also uses a database
The outbox insert makes the whole transfer commit faster than a plain transaction
It avoids the dual-write problem: transfer and event commit or fail together
The outbox table replaces the ledger as the source of truth for every balance
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Publishing after the commit can fail after the money moved, so the event is lost; publishing first can announce a transfer that rolled back. The outbox commits atomically, and a relay publishes at least once.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: A user sends 100 USD from a USD wallet to a EUR wallet. How should the ledger record it so that every currency still balances?
options: Debit 100 USD and credit the EUR equivalent as one entry pair that does not sum to zero
Convert both wallets to USD for the duration of the transfer, then convert back after
Store the amount as a float in a neutral reference currency and convert on every read
Route via house USD and EUR accounts at a locked quote, so each currency sums to zero
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Double entry only balances within one currency, so FX goes through house accounts per currency, with the conversion at a locked quote. A USD debit paired with a EUR credit cannot sum to zero, and reconciliation would flag every FX transfer.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Each ledger entry stores balance_after. Select all statements that are correct.
options: It lets you read a wallet's balance at any past point without replaying all history
Gaps or jumps between consecutive entries' balance_after values reveal a missing or corrupt entry
It must be computed in the same transaction as the wallet balance update
It can be edited later if a mistake is found, since it is only a convenience field
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: balance_after makes point-in-time reads cheap and enables chain checks, but it is only trustworthy if written atomically with the balance change. Ledger rows are immutable; mistakes are corrected with compensating entries.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: The external payment provider sends signed settlement webhooks for top-ups. Select all sound handling practices.
options: Verify the webhook signature before trusting the payload
Deduplicate by the provider's event id, since webhooks can be delivered more than once
Drive the top-up through a status state machine so out-of-order events cannot move it backwards
Credit the wallet as soon as the user submits the top-up, before the provider confirms
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Authenticate, deduplicate and order-protect webhook processing. Crediting before confirmation invents money that may never arrive.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: In the event-sourced variant, wallets take periodic snapshots. Select all statements that are correct.
options: Snapshots speed up rebuilding state by replaying only events after the snapshot
A snapshot must record the last sequence number it includes
Events stay immutable; schema changes are handled with versioned events or upcasters
Once a snapshot exists, older events can be deleted, since the snapshot contains everything
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Snapshots are an optimisation tied to a sequence position, and immutable events need versioning to evolve. Deleting history would destroy the audit trail and the ability to recompute balances at any point in time.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Because every transfer's ledger entries sum to zero, the total money across all wallets and external clearing accounts is conserved by construction.
options: True
False
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: True. Each debit has an equal credit, so money only moves between accounts; money entering or leaving the system shows up as entries on external or clearing accounts.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: A read replica is a safe source for the balance used to approve a transfer, because replication lag is usually under a second.
options: True
False
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: False. Even a small lag can show a stale, higher balance and allow an overdraft. The approval check must use the primary, ideally the conditional UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= amount itself.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: The sequenced event log grows by about 100 GB per trading day, and regulators require 7 years of retention. With about 252 trading days a year, roughly how much log is that?
options: About 25 TB
About 176 TB
About 256 TB
About 1.8 PB
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: 100 GB x 252 is about 25 TB per year; x7 is about 176 TB. 256 TB uses 365 days, but the exchange only trades on trading days.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: An order spends 8 us in gateway decode and risk, 2 us in the sequencer, 3 us matching and 4 us publishing to the outbound path. What is the internal wire-to-wire latency?
options: About 8 us
About 17 us
About 34 us
About 170 us
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: The stages are sequential on the order's path: 8 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 17 us, comfortably inside a well-under-100 us budget. Taking only the largest stage (8 us) ignores that stages add up.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: The ask side holds 100 @ 10.01, 150 @ 10.02 and 200 @ 10.03. A market buy order for 300 arrives. Which fills result?
options: 300 @ 10.02, the average price
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: A market order walks the book from the best ask: it takes all 100 at 10.01, all 150 at 10.02, then 50 of the 200 at 10.03, each at the resting order's price. Only 100 shares exist at 10.01, so 300 @ 10.01 is impossible.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: The ask side holds 120 @ 9.99 and 100 @ 10.01. An IOC buy limit order for 200 @ 10.00 arrives. What happens?
options: 120 fill at 9.99 and the remaining 80 are cancelled
Nothing fills, since the whole 200 is not available within the limit
120 fill at 9.99 and the remaining 80 rest on the bid at 10.00
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: IOC fills whatever is available within its limit immediately and cancels the rest; 10.01 is above the 10.00 limit. Resting the remainder is what a plain DAY limit order would do, and 'all or nothing' is FOK.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: The ask side holds 100 @ 10.01, 100 @ 10.02 and 200 @ 10.03. A FOK buy limit order for 250 @ 10.02 arrives. What happens?
options: 200 fill immediately and the remaining 50 rest on the bid at 10.02
250 fill, with the last 50 taken at 10.03 to complete the order
No fills: only 200 are available at or below 10.02, so it is killed
200 fill immediately and the remaining 50 are cancelled right away
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Fill-or-kill executes in full immediately or not at all. Only 200 shares are offered at or below 10.02, so it is killed with no trades. Partially filling and cancelling the rest is IOC behaviour.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: A trader's cancel and an incoming order that would fill the same resting order arrive at nearly the same moment. How does the exchange resolve the race?
options: The cancel always wins, whatever the arrival order, to protect the trader
The fill always wins, whatever the arrival order, since trades matter more
The engine runs both in parallel threads and keeps whichever finishes first
Sequencer order decides; if the fill came first, the cancel is late or partial
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: The sequencer defines one global order, and the deterministic engine applies events in that order, so the outcome is fair and replayable. A fixed 'cancel wins' rule would require reordering events, which breaks determinism.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: When is a tick-indexed array a better choice than a sorted tree for a symbol's price levels?
options: When a price band bounds the ticks, so each level is a direct O(1) index
When prices can range over many orders of magnitude during a session
When the implementation language has no balanced tree in its library
When nearly all incoming orders are market orders rather than limits
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: An array indexed by price tick gives O(1) access to any level but needs a bounded range of ticks, which price bands provide. For unbounded or very wide ranges the array would be huge and sparse, so a tree's O(log n) is the better trade.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: A matching engine written in a garbage-collected language allocates a new object for every order and shows p99 latency spikes of several milliseconds every few seconds. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Network jitter between gateways and engine; add more gateways to spread the load
GC pauses; pre-allocate orders and events in pools or a ring buffer instead
Too few symbols per engine; merge engines so each one stays busy and warm
The journal is too slow under load; turn journaling off on the hot path
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Periodic multi-millisecond stalls in an allocating hot path are classic GC pauses; pre-allocation and object reuse, as in the LMAX Disruptor, remove them. Disabling journaling would break durability and replay.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: A market data client receives incremental update seq 1001 and then seq 1004. What should it do?
options: Apply 1004 and carry on, since the missing updates were most likely duplicates
Ask the matching engine itself to resend its whole order log from the start
Distrust its book, fetch a snapshot or retransmission, then reapply increments
Average updates 1001 and 1004 to estimate the contents of the missing updates
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Feed sequence numbers exist to detect gaps; applying later increments onto a book that missed updates gives wrong depth. Recovery uses a snapshot or retransmission service, never the engine itself.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: The exchange must support market-wide halts and opening auctions. Select all statements that are correct.
options: Halt and resume are submitted as sequenced events, so replay reproduces exactly when matching stopped
During an auction call period orders are collected without continuous matching
An auction typically uncrosses at a single price chosen to maximise executed volume
In an opening auction, each order executes at its own limit price in arrival order
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Putting halts in the sequenced stream keeps the engine deterministic, and auctions collect orders, then execute all crossing orders at one uniform clearing price. Executing each at its own limit would be continuous matching, not an auction.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: Select all characteristics of an LMAX Disruptor style pipeline in the matching engine.
options: A pre-allocated ring buffer replaces locked queues between stages
Stages coordinate through sequence numbers instead of locks
Journaling and replication run in parallel with the business-logic stage
Each stage allocates a fresh message object per event to avoid sharing memory
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: The ring buffer is allocated once and its slots are reused, which avoids GC and lock contention; consumers track sequences, and durability stages run alongside matching. Per-event allocation is exactly what the design avoids.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: One very hot symbol alone approaches the capacity of the engine it shares with other symbols. Select all sound responses.
options: Give that symbol its own dedicated sequencer and engine pair
Optimise the hot path (pinned cores, cache-friendly structures) since one thread can handle millions of events per second
Hash that symbol's orders across four engines by order id
Move the other symbols off its engine to other engine pairs
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: One book must be matched by one deterministic engine to keep price-time priority, so you isolate it and make that engine faster. Splitting one symbol's orders across engines means no engine sees the whole book, so orders that should cross would not match.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: Prices are stored as integer ticks rather than floating point, so that price comparisons and level lookups are exact.
options: True
False
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: True. Floating-point rounding could make two equal prices compare unequal and place orders on the wrong level; integer ticks are exact and fast.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: When an incoming limit order crosses the book, the trades execute at the incoming order's limit price.
options: True
False
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: False. Trades execute at the resting order's price; the incoming order's limit only bounds how far it can walk the book. A buy limit at 10.05 against an ask at 10.01 trades at 10.01.
